title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
5.3 Multiple comparisons across 88 counties
Section 4.1.5 classified 16 counties as significant at p < 0.05 and mapped them.
A LISA map involves one hypothesis test per county. Each test is evaluated at α = 0.05, the probability of a false positive for a single test. With no spatial pattern present, 88 tests evaluated at 0.05 are expected to produce about four significant counties. Section 3.5 met the problem of multiple comparisons on a smaller scale: with six correlogram lags tested in one table, lag 3 was no longer significant after Holm’s correction.
A correction for multiple comparisons raises the evidence a test must reach, so that a county is called significant only on stronger evidence than 0.05. Neither chapter applies one. Both assigned papers on the local statistics state that a correction is needed: Anselin (1995), which introduced the local Moran, and Ord and Getis (1995), on the distribution of Gi and Gi*. They disagree over how many tests the correction should count, and section 5.3.1 sets out the disagreement. Two corrections are used here, both taken from the readings:

Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests, so every county is evaluated at 0.05/88, the same fixed penalty for all. Ord and Getis (1995) recommend it, and Anselin (1995) applies it in his worked example.
Benjamini-Hochberg is less severe. It controls the false discovery rate (FDR), the expected proportion of false positives among the rejections, and rejects the ith smallest p-value when p(i) ≤ i × 0.05 / 88, so its threshold increases with rank. Getis (2010) cites it, from Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), among the attempts to address multiple testing in local statistics.

How many of the 16 counties remain significant after each correction, and which conclusions does the map then support?

p <- lisa$p_ii_sim
tibble(correction = c("none", "Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR)", "Bonferroni"),
       significant = c(sum(p < 0.05),
                       sum(p.adjust(p, method = "fdr") < 0.05),
                       sum(p.adjust(p, method = "bonferroni") < 0.05))) |>
  kable()

The block uses one new function:
p.adjust(p, method = p.adjust.methods)                    # stats

p.adjust() adjusts a set of p-values for multiple comparisons, so that each adjusted value can be compared directly with 0.05.
method = "bonferroni" multiplies each p-value by the number of tests, 88, with a ceiling of 1.
method = "fdr" applies the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.
sum(... < 0.05) counts the counties whose adjusted p-value is below 0.05.




Under either correction, none of the 88 counties remains significant, and no county on the LISA map meets a corrected threshold at this number of simulations.
This follows from the smallest p-value that 999 permutations can produce (section 5.2).

c(floor_at_nsim_999 = min(lisa$p_ii_sim), bonferroni_threshold = 0.05 / 88)

The block uses two new functions:
st_drop_geometry(x)                                       # sf

st_drop_geometry() removes the geometry column, which turns the sf object into an ordinary data frame and keeps the printed table short.
filter() keeps the rows for which the condition is true, here the counties whose FDR-adjusted p-value is below 0.05.
select() (section 2.3) then keeps the five columns printed.





5.3.1 Size of the Bonferroni correction
These counts give the number of counties that remain significant under each correction. They do not determine whether a correction should be applied to a LISA map at all. Two positions are possible. If the map is treated as exploratory, each county’s p-value describes only that county and no correction is required. If the map is treated as 88 simultaneous tests, a correction is required and the remaining question is its size. Neither chapter discusses whether a correction should be applied. Anselin (1995) and Ord and Getis (1995) both take the second position.
Ord and Getis (1995) recommend the Bonferroni correction:

we believe that the limits given by the Bonferroni inequality, possibly with the Tukey approximation, represent a reasonable basis for making inferences until more precise methods are developed.

They also record a referee’s objection in the same paragraph: “One of the referees has noted that the Bonferroni limits may be unduly conservative when n becomes large. This issue needs to be explored further.”
Anselin (1995) agrees that a correction is needed and questions its size:

Due to this correlation, and the associated problem of multiple comparisons, the usual interpretation of significance will be flawed.


while it is obvious that some correction to the individual significance levels is needed, the extent to which it is indeed necessary to take m = n remains to be further investigated.

His reason is that the dependence between local statistics is local and bounded: “the number of common neighbors does not change with the number of observations”. He notes that on a regular lattice under the Queen rule, first-order neighbours share four elements of their neighbourhood sets, second-order neighbours three, and higher-order neighbours none. Setting m, the number of tests, equal to n, the number of observations, therefore corrects for more tests than are correlated with one another.
He nevertheless applies m = n in his own worked example on 42 African countries: “the individual significance levels for each observation should be taken as 0.05/42, or 0.0012.”
Getis (2010), a chapter on the Lesson 5 reference list, returns to multiple testing in local statistics fifteen years later. He describes the selection of tests that can withstand “the simultaneity effects of multiple tests” as “a particularly difficult area of research”, since the observations used for one local test are used again for the tests at neighbouring locations, and cites Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) and Castro and Singer (2006) among the attempts to resolve it. The Benjamini-Hochberg counts above are reported alongside Bonferroni because Getis (2010) cites that procedure as one of these attempts.


5.3.2 Permutation count and the p-value floor
Anselin’s worked example is also relevant to the choice of nsim. A corrected bound cannot be met by a p-value whose minimum attainable value exceeds it, so the number of permutations should be chosen after the correction. Anselin used 9,999 conditional permutations and gives no reason for choosing 9,999 rather than some smaller number. His bound is 0.05/42 = 0.0012, and a minimum p-value of 1/(nsim+1) falls below that bound from about nsim = 840 upwards, so the arithmetic does not require a count that high. At 9,999 permutations the minimum is well below his bound:

only Sudan meeting the Bonferroni bound for an overall a = 0.05. For this country, two out of the 9,999 statistics computed from the randomized samples exceed the observed one, clearly labeling the latter as “extreme.”

Chapter 10 sets nsim = 99 before any correction is considered.

tibble(setting = c("chapter 10, nsim = 99", "this page, nsim = 999",
                   "section 5.3, nsim = 9999", "Anselin (1995), nsim = 9999, n = 42"),
       floor = c(2/100, 2/1000, 2/10000, 1/10000),
       bonferroni_bound = c(0.05/88, 0.05/88, 0.05/88, 0.05/42)) |>
  mutate(correction_reachable = floor < bonferroni_bound) |>
  kable(digits = 5)

At chapter 10’s setting the minimum attainable p-value (0.02) is about thirty-five times the Bonferroni bound for 88 counties (0.00057), so no county can be significant after the correction, whatever the data.


5.3.3 Counties significant after correction
Earlier in this section, no county remained significant under either correction at nsim = 999, and three remained significant under FDR at 9,999. Two decisions follow for the LISA map of section 4.1.5 and the hot and cold spot map of section 4.2.3: whether to redraw them at a corrected threshold, and which claims the text around them can support.
The map in section 4.1.5 is left uncorrected and treated as exploratory, so that each county’s p-value describes only that county, the first of the two positions in section 5.3.1. The counts above report how many of its counties a correction would retain.
The two maps below use the same 9,999 permutations, so they differ only in the correction.


Code
lvls <- c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")
lisa_corr <- lisa |>
  mutate(uncorrected = factor(ifelse(lm_big$p_ii_sim < 0.05,
                                     as.character(mean), "Insignificant"), levels = lvls),
         fdr = factor(ifelse(p.adjust(lm_big$p_ii_sim, "fdr") < 0.05,
                             as.character(mean), "Insignificant"), levels = lvls))

cluster_map <- function(col, title) {
  tm_shape(lisa_corr) +
    tm_polygons(fill = col,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                  values = c("grey80", "blue", "lightblue", "pink", "red")),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA cluster",
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
    tm_title(title)
}

tmap_arrange(cluster_map("uncorrected", "No correction, 17 counties"),
             cluster_map("fdr", "Benjamini-Hochberg, 3 counties"),
             asp = 1, ncol = 2)









Three counties remain after correction: Longhui and Wugang, Low-Low counties in the west, and Xiangtan, in the High-High cluster around Changsha. Wugang is the only county that also meets the Bonferroni bound. The corrected map is therefore weighted towards the Low-Low cluster in the west, which reverses the emphasis of the uncorrected map. The 16 counties of section 4.1.5 are candidate clusters. The Gi* map of section 4.2.3 was not tested against a corrected threshold.
The corrected result also differs from global G in section 5.4, which indicates that high values dominate the province-wide pattern. The two results are consistent because the statistics measure different things. Global G weights counties by the magnitude of their values. A corrected LISA identifies the individual counties whose statistics meet a threshold corrected for 88 simultaneous tests, and two of the three such counties have low GDPPC.
Anselin (1995) raises a further point that no correction addresses. Local statistics are themselves spatially autocorrelated, since neighbouring counties share the observations from which their statistics are computed:

This spatial clustering (or spatial autocorrelation) of both the Gi* and the LISA statistics is a result of the way they are constructed, and should be kept in mind when visually interpreting a map of LISAs.

When significant counties are adjacent, the map cannot show whether they reflect a pattern shared across the area or one very high value that falls in all of their neighbourhoods.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
5.4 Getis-Ord global G
Sections 3.3 and 3.4 found positive spatial autocorrelation in GDPPC under both global measures (Moran’s I = 0.301, Geary’s C = 0.691). Neither statistic distinguishes clustering of high values from clustering of low values.
The Getis-Ord global G, covered in slides 16 and 17 but in neither chapter, measures the overall concentration of high or low values. Getis and Ord (1992) state the limitation of Moran’s I that G addresses:

The I(d) statistic has its peculiar weakness in not being able to discriminate between patterns that have high values dominant within d or low values dominant.

Getis and Ord (1992) conclude that “any test for spatial association should use both types of statistics.”
Does the positive spatial autocorrelation in GDPPC reflect clustering of high values or of low values?

nb_band <- dnearneigh(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan)), 0, ct)
lw_band <- nb2listw(nb_band, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
globalG.test(hunan$GDPPC, lw_band, zero.policy = TRUE)


    Getis-Ord global G statistic

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: lw_band   

standard deviate = 3.0285, p-value = 0.001229
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Global G statistic        Expectation           Variance 
      5.099677e-02       4.362591e-02       5.923594e-06 








NoteHow the code works





The block uses three new functions:
st_centroid(x)                                            # sf
dnearneigh(x, d1, d2)                                     # spdep
globalG.test(x, listw, zero.policy = attr(listw, "zero.policy"),
             alternative = "greater")                     # spdep

st_centroid() replaces each county by its centroid, and dnearneigh() makes every pair of centroids between d1 = 0 and d2 = ct metres apart into neighbours.
nb2listw(style = "B") gives each neighbour a weight of 1 without row standardisation, as the definition of G requires.
globalG.test() computes G and tests it against its expectation under spatial randomness. alternative = "greater", the default, tests whether high values are concentrated.




Getis and Ord (1992) define G on a binary distance-based weights matrix, so style = "B" follows from the definition of the statistic. G is the ratio of the weighted sum of the products of value pairs to the total sum of the products of value pairs. Only the numerator contains the weights, so row standardisation would change the meaning of the ratio.
For GDPPC, G is 0.0510, against an expectation of 0.0436 (z = 3.03, p = 0.0012). A significant positive z-score indicates that high values within d of other high values dominate the pattern.
This appears to conflict with the LISA map of section 4.1.5, which has nine Low-Low counties and six High-High counties. The two statistics measure different things:

mu <- mean(hunan$GDPPC)
lisa |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(LISA_cluster %in% c("High-High", "Low-Low")) |>
  group_by(LISA_cluster) |>
  summarise(counties = n(),
            mean_deviation_from_provincial_mean = round(mean(GDPPC - mu))) |>
  kable()

counties

NoteHow the code works





The block uses three new functions:
group_by(.data, ...)                                      # dplyr
summarise(.data, ...)                                     # dplyr
n()                                                       # dplyr

filter() (section 5.3) keeps the High-High and Low-Low counties.
group_by() splits the rows by cluster, and summarise() then computes one row per group.
n() counts the counties in each group, and mean(GDPPC - mu) averages their deviation from the provincial mean, mu.




Global G weights each county by the magnitude of its value. On average the six High-High counties are about 28,900 yuan above the provincial mean, and the nine Low-Low counties about 11,600 yuan below it. GDPPC is bounded below by zero and unbounded above, so high values deviate further from the mean than low values, and they dominate a sum-of-products statistic although they are fewer.
The three statistics therefore describe different aspects of the same pattern. Moran’s I indicates positive spatial autocorrelation, global G indicates that high values dominate it, and the LISA map shows where the clusters are: high values around Changsha and low values in the west.

5.4.1 Natural origin and location invariance
Section 4.1.4 standardised GDPPC before plotting it against its spatial lag, because the scatterplot compares each county with the provincial mean. Chapter 10 standardises there but computes Gi* on the raw values, and does not say why the two differ. The reason is a condition that Getis and Ord (1992) place on G, and that neither chapter states.
A variable has a natural origin when zero represents the absence of the quantity measured, as opposed to an arbitrary reference point. G is computed from the values themselves, not from their deviations from the mean, so the position of zero on the measurement scale affects the statistic. GDPPC has a natural origin, since zero yuan per person corresponds to zero output. Regression residuals do not, since their zero is defined by the fitted line.
Getis and Ord (1992) state two conditions, the first for Gi and the second for G(d):

Gi is scale-invariant (Yi = bXi yields the same scores as Xi) but not location-invariant (Yi = a + Xi gives different results than Xi). The statistic is intended for use only for those variables that possess a natural origin.


it is inappropriate to use G(d) to study residuals from regression.

How far do G and Moran’s I change when a constant is added to GDPPC?

shift_test <- function(a) {
  x <- hunan$GDPPC + a
  g <- globalG.test(x, lw_band, zero.policy = TRUE)
  m <- moran.test(x, rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE)
  tibble(shift = a, G = g$estimate[1], z_G = g$statistic, p_G = g$p.value,
         I = m$estimate[1], z_I = m$statistic, p_I = m$p.value)
}
bind_rows(shift_test(0), shift_test(10000), shift_test(100000)) |>
  mutate(across(c(p_G, p_I), ~ format(.x, digits = 3, scientific = TRUE))) |>
  kable(digits = 4)

The block defines one function and uses two new ones:

bind_rows(...)                                            # dplyr
across(.cols, .fns)                                       # dplyr

shift_test() adds a constant a to GDPPC, runs global G and Moran’s I on the shifted values, and returns one row of results. Defining it once means the three shifts are computed in exactly the same way.
bind_rows() stacks the three one-row results into one table.
across(c(p_G, p_I), ~ format(...)) applies the same formatting to both p-value columns, which prints the very small values in scientific notation.




Moran’s I is unchanged: it is computed on deviations from the mean, and adding a constant leaves every deviation unchanged. Global G is no longer significant. Its z-score decreases from 3.03 to 0.90 and its p-value increases from 0.0012 to 0.19. Multiplying GDPPC by a constant, in place of adding one, leaves both statistics unchanged. This is the scale invariance that Getis and Ord describe.

g2 <- globalG.test(hunan$GDPPC * 2, lw_band, zero.policy = TRUE)
m2 <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC * 2, rswm_q, zero.policy = TRUE)
c(G_doubled = g2$estimate[1], z_G_doubled = g2$statistic,
  I_doubled = m2$estimate[1], z_I_doubled = m2$statistic)

The natural-origin requirement makes a G result a statement about the variable on the scale on which it was measured. For a variable centred at zero, or for regression residuals, a significant G would be an artefact of the position of zero on the scale.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
5.5 Null models for Moran’s I
Section 3.3.1 ran moran.test() on GDPPC and reported a z-score of 4.74. Moran (1950), who introduced the statistic, states that its variance, and so this z-score, requires normally distributed values, and GDPPC is right skewed. By default, however, moran.test() does not use Moran’s variance. Its randomisation argument, which defaults to TRUE and is not mentioned in either chapter, selects a different null model. What does each null model assume?
Moran (1950) derives the expectation of I without any distributional assumption, and states that the second moment (which gives the variance, how widely I spreads around its expectation) requires an assumption about the distribution:

To evaluate the second moment of I we have to assume further that all the xij are distributed normally.

randomisation = FALSE is Moran’s own variance, which assumes the values are drawn from a normal distribution. Geary (1954) sets out both null models:

The theory is discussed from the viewpoints of both randomization and classical normal theory. With the randomization approach, the observations themselves are the “universe” and no assumption need be made as to the character of the frequency distribution.

Having found the distribution of c close to normal for Ireland’s 26 counties, he concludes that “accordingly, one can have confidence in deciding on significance from the standard error.”

Normality assumes the 88 values are drawn from a normal distribution, which does not hold for a right-skewed variable such as GDPPC.
Randomisation, the default used in section 3.3.1, treats the 88 values as fixed and considers every assignment of them to counties. Its z-score still relies on a normal approximation.
Permutation, used in section 3.3.2, samples 999 of those assignments and needs no approximation.

Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2 reach the same conclusion under the randomisation and permutation null models: both reject the null hypothesis of no spatial autocorrelation. I is a sum over all 88 counties, so a normal approximation suits it better than a local statistic computed from five neighbours, which is the case examined in section 5.2.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
5.6 Local Geary’s c
Section 3.4 computed Geary’s C for the whole province. Section 3.5 compared its correlogram with that of Moran’s I, and the two differed in significance at lags 3 and 6.
Neither chapter computes the local form of Geary’s C. Slide 26 identifies it as a second LISA, alongside local Moran’s I. Each of the two local statistics misses a pattern that the other detects, and this section compares them on GDPPC.
Local Moran’s I and local Geary’s c differ in construction. Up to scaling constants, for county \(i\) with neighbours \(j\) and weights \(w_{ij}\),
\[
I_i = (x_i - \bar{x}) \sum_j w_{ij}(x_j - \bar{x}), \qquad c_i = \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 .
\]

Local Moran’s I compares the county with the provincial mean. It multiplies the county’s deviation from the mean by the weighted deviations of its neighbours, so for a county near the mean \(I_i\) is small, even when the county matches its neighbours closely.
Local Geary’s c compares the county with its neighbours. As slide 26 defines it, \(c_i\) adds up the squared differences between the county and each neighbour, and the provincial mean cancels in each difference. \(c_i\) is large for a county whose value differs sharply from its neighbours’ values. It cannot distinguish High-High from Low-Low, since a cluster of high values and a cluster of low values both give small differences.

Section 4.1.5 found 16 significant counties with local Moran’s I. How many does local Geary’s c find, and which counties do the two statistics classify differently?

set.seed(1234)
lgeary <- wm_q |>
  mutate(local_c = local_c_perm(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |>
  unnest(local_c)

tibble(statistic = c("local Moran's I", "local Geary's c"),
       significant_at_0.05 = c(sum(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05),
                               sum(lgeary$p_ci_sim < 0.05))) |>
  kable()

The block uses one new function:

local_c_perm() computes local Geary’s c for each county and tests it by conditional permutation. It follows the pattern of local_moran() in section 4.1.2: it returns a data frame of results, stored as the column local_c and spread into columns by unnest().
p_ci_sim is the rank-based p-value from the 999 permutations. nsim defaults to 499.




Local Geary’s c identifies 21 significant counties, against 16 for local Moran’s I. Eleven counties are significant under one statistic and not the other.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
section: 5.7 Gi* weights: fixed band versus k nearest neighbours
text:
5.7 Gi* weights: fixed band versus k nearest neighbours
Section 4.2.1 created hunan_adw as chapter 10 does, but chapter 10 never uses it. Section 4.2.2 computed Gi* on the fixed distance band only.
Fixed and adaptive schemes hold different quantities constant:

A fixed distance band fixes the radius. One radius applies to the whole province, so a county surrounded by large counties has few neighbours, and a county in an area of small counties has many.
An adaptive scheme fixes the number of neighbours. Every county has the same number, and the radius varies.

The maps below show this for two counties: Yuanling, a large county in the west, and Shaodong, a smaller one in the centre.


Code
show_nb <- function(nb, title) {
  yl <- which(hunan$County == "Yuanling")
  sd <- which(hunan$County == "Shaodong")
  hunan |>
    mutate(group = case_when(row_number() %in% nb[[yl]] ~ "Yuanling and its neighbours",
                             row_number() %in% nb[[sd]] ~ "Shaodong and its neighbours",
                             TRUE ~ "Other"),
           group = factor(group, levels = c("Yuanling and its neighbours",
                                            "Shaodong and its neighbours", "Other"))) |>
    tm_shape() +
    tm_polygons(fill = "group",
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("purple", "orange", "grey90")),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "", position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
    tm_title(title)
}

tmap_arrange(show_nb(hunan_fdw$nb, "Fixed band, 62,955 m"),
             show_nb(hunan_adw$nb, "Adaptive, k = 6 plus self"),
             asp = 1, ncol = 2)









For Gi*, reported as a z-score, the number of neighbours matters. According to slide 30, a sparse neighbourhood produces a large variance of the estimate, which reduces the z-score of Gi* towards zero, so the county is less likely to reach significance. Slide 35 gives a rule of thumb of about eight neighbours per feature for a skewed variable.
How many counties do the two schemes classify differently, and are the differences mainly in one direction?

set.seed(1234)
HCSA_adw <- hunan_adw |>
  mutate(gistar = local_gstar_perm(GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |>
  unnest(gistar) |>
  mutate(HCSA_cluster = case_when(p_sim >= signif ~ "Insignificant",
                                  gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
                                  TRUE ~ "Cold spot"),
         HCSA_cluster = factor(HCSA_cluster,
                               levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")))

table(fixed_band = HCSA_fdw$HCSA_cluster,
      adaptive_k = HCSA_adw$HCSA_cluster)

               adaptive_k
fixed_band      Insignificant Hot spot Cold spot
  Insignificant            65        5         6
  Hot spot                  1        6         0
  Cold spot                 3        0         2


The two schemes classify 15 of the 88 counties differently, and most of the differences are in one direction:

Eleven counties are significant under the adaptive weights and not under the fixed band.
Four are significant under the fixed band and not under the adaptive weights.

The map below is the adaptive counterpart of the map in section 4.2.3.

tm_shape(HCSA_adw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "HCSA_cluster",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
                values = c("grey80", "red", "blue")),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* cluster",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_title("Hot and cold spots of GDPPC, adaptive k = 6 plus self, p < 0.05")









tibble(scheme = c("fixed band", "adaptive k"),
       min_neighbours = c(min(lengths(hunan_fdw$nb)), min(lengths(hunan_adw$nb))),
       median_neighbours = c(median(lengths(hunan_fdw$nb)), median(lengths(hunan_adw$nb))),
       max_neighbours = c(max(lengths(hunan_fdw$nb)), max(lengths(hunan_adw$nb)))) |>
  kable()

The neighbour counts explain the direction of the differences:

Fixed band: as few as two neighbours. Some counties have as few as two neighbours, including themselves, which is the sparse case described on slide 30. The median county has five.
Adaptive: seven for every county. No county has a small neighbourhood because of its location among large counties. Seven is also close to the eight suggested on slide 35.

The adaptive scheme looks preferable, but a larger count of significant counties does not show that a scheme is more accurate. A larger neighbourhood alone produces more significant counties, with no change in the data: more neighbours lower the variance of Gi* (slide 30), which moves its z-score away from zero. The eight neighbours of slide 35 is a guideline. Section 5.7.1 therefore varies k and checks which classifications change.

5.7.1 Sensitivity to the number of neighbours
Section 4.2.1 set k = 6 as chapter 10 does, and the comparison above uses that value alone.
Mack and Kam (2018) take a different approach to the same decision in their study of conflict in Africa. Before choosing a weights matrix, they tabulate two quantities under several definitions:

the number of regions left without neighbours;
the average number of links.

They reject the widest definition because an average of 52 links “may skew the analysis”.
The same check can be applied to k. A county whose Gi* classification is the same under several neighbourhood sizes depends less on any one of them.
How many counties are significant at k = 4, 6 and 8, and which keep the same classification under all three?

nb_k4 <- include_self(st_knn(st_geometry(hunan), k = 4))
set.seed(1234)
gi_k4 <- local_gstar_perm(hunan$GDPPC, nb_k4, st_weights(nb_k4), nsim = 999)

nb_k8 <- include_self(st_knn(st_geometry(hunan), k = 8))
set.seed(1234)
gi_k8 <- local_gstar_perm(hunan$GDPPC, nb_k8, st_weights(nb_k8), nsim = 999)

k_compare <- tibble(
  County = hunan$County,
  k4 = case_when(gi_k4$p_sim >= signif ~ "Insignificant",
                 gi_k4$gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot", TRUE ~ "Cold spot"),
  k6 = as.character(HCSA_adw$HCSA_cluster),
  k8 = case_when(gi_k8$p_sim >= signif ~ "Insignificant",
                 gi_k8$gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot", TRUE ~ "Cold spot"))

tibble(k = c(4, 6, 8),
       significant_counties = c(sum(k_compare$k4 != "Insignificant"),
                                sum(k_compare$k6 != "Insignificant"),
                                sum(k_compare$k8 != "Insignificant"))) |>
  kable()

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
section: 5.8 Gi and local Moran’s I under permutation
text:
5.8 Gi and local Moran’s I under permutation
Section 4.1 produced a LISA map from the local Moran and section 4.2 a hot and cold spot map from Gi*. Chapter 10 presents the two as separate analyses.
Anselin (1995) argues that the two share one permutation test:

Under conditional permutation, only the numerator of each statistic varies.
The varying term is the same in both statistics.
Therefore:

the randomization method applied to [the local Moran] will yield the same empirical reference distribution as when applied to the Getis and Ord Gi and Gi* statistics. Hence, inference based on this nonparametric approach will be identical for the two statistics.


On the Queen contiguity weights of section 4.1.1, do Gi and Gi* give the same permutation p-values as the local Moran? A second run of Gi* with a different random seed shows how much two runs differ by chance alone.

set.seed(7); li  <- local_moran(hunan$GDPPC, wm_q$nb, wm_q$wt, nsim = 9999)
set.seed(7); gi  <- local_g_perm(hunan$GDPPC, wm_q$nb, wm_q$wt, nsim = 9999)
set.seed(7); gs  <- local_gstar_perm(hunan$GDPPC, wm_q$nb, wm_q$wt, nsim = 9999)
set.seed(8); gs2 <- local_gstar_perm(hunan$GDPPC, wm_q$nb, wm_q$wt, nsim = 9999)

tibble(comparison = c("Gi against local Moran",
                      "Gi* against local Moran",
                      "Gi* against Gi*, different random seed"),
       largest_difference = c(max(abs(gi$p_sim - li$p_ii_sim)),
                              max(abs(gs$p_sim - li$p_ii_sim)),
                              max(abs(gs$p_sim - gs2$p_sim))),
       counties_significant_in_one_only = c(
         sum((gi$p_sim < signif) != (li$p_ii_sim < signif)),
         sum((gs$p_sim < signif) != (li$p_ii_sim < signif)),
         sum((gs$p_sim < signif) != (gs2$p_sim < signif)))) |>
  kable(digits = 4)









comparison
largest_difference
counties_significant_in_one_only




Gi against local Moran
0.0002
0


Gi* against local Moran
0.0328
1


Gi* against Gi*, different random seed
0.0290
0











NoteHow the code works





The block uses one new function:
local_g_perm(x, nb, wt, nsim = 499, alternative = "two.sided")   # sfdep

local_g_perm() computes Gi, which excludes the county itself, where local_gstar_perm() (section 4.2.2) computes Gi*, which includes it. All three statistics use the Queen contiguity weights of section 4.1.1 and 9,999 permutations.
set.seed() (section 3.3.2) before each call starts every statistic from the same random numbers, except the second Gi* run, which uses a different seed to measure simulation error.
abs() takes absolute differences, and max() keeps the largest across the 88 counties.





Gi agrees with the local Moran to within 0.0002, one step of the p-value grid at 9,999 permutations.
Gi* differs from the local Moran by up to 0.033, but two runs of Gi* differ from each other by a similar amount, 0.029.

The difference between Gi* and the local Moran is therefore simulation error, and Anselin’s (1995) claim holds for both Gi and Gi* on these data.
Gi* and the local Moran also reach the same decision at p < 0.05 for every county except Yongshun, whose p-value is 0.051 under the local Moran and 0.047 under Gi*. A difference of that size lies within the simulation error shown in the table.
Where Gi* and the local Moran give the same p-value, they differ in what a significant result says about the county:

The local Moran identifies similarity and outliers. A significant positive local Moran indicates that the county and its neighbours have similar values, without indicating whether those values are high or low. The local Moran also identifies the High-Low and Low-High outliers, which Gi* does not.
Gi* indicates whether the values are high or low. A positive value marks a cluster of high values and a negative value a cluster of low values (Anselin 1995).

This is the sense of the recommendation by Getis and Ord (1992) in section 5.4 that “any test for spatial association should use both types of statistics”.
On the same weights, the permutation tests behind chapter 10’s LISA map and hot and cold spot map would give the same p-values. The two maps differ for two reasons: they use different weights, Queen contiguity against a fixed distance band, and they classify the significant counties differently.
